title: Hypotension Prediction Index versus Mean Arterial Pressure Alarm for Preventing Intraoperative Hypotension in Elective Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Anna A. Florax; Marijn P. Mulder; Roland P. van Ieperen; Libera Fresiello et al.
abstract: Background: Intraoperative hypotension is common during surgery and has been retrospectively associated with acute kidney injury, myocardial injury, and increased mortality. The Hypotension Prediction Index was developed to support proactive blood pressure management but shows a strong correlation with mean arterial pressure. Observational data suggest that a mean arterial pressure alarm set at 72 mmHg may perform similarly to the default Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (greater than 85). The authors hypothesized that a 72 mmHg mean arterial pressure alarm is noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index in preventing intraoperative hypotension. Methods: In this single-center, blinded, randomized controlled trial, adults undergoing moderate- or high-risk elective noncardiac surgery with continuous arterial pressure monitoring were assigned to either a mean arterial pressure alarm (less than 72 mmHg) or a Hypotension Prediction Index alarm (greater than 85). The primary outcome was the area under the threshold for mean arterial pressure less than 65 mmHg. Secondary outcomes included the incidence and severity of hypo- and hypertension, duration of active alarms, incidence of acute kidney and myocardial injury, 30-day mortality, hospital length of stay, and cumulative dosages of vasoactive medication and fluids. Results: A total of 143 participants were included in the final analysis. The median [IQR] area under the hypotension threshold was 3.75 [0.00 to 22.62] mmHg ⋅ min in the mean arterial pressure group and 4.00 [0.00 to 19.00] mmHg ⋅ min in the Hypotension Prediction Index group. After log-transformation, the mean difference was 0.03 (95% CI, −0.24 to 0.29), with the lower bound remaining above the predefined noninferiority margin (−0.4). No differences were observed in secondary hemodynamic metrics, alarm characteristics, patient outcomes, or administered medications and fluids. Conclusion: A mean arterial pressure alarm of 72 mmHg is noninferior to the Hypotension Prediction Index greater than 85 in preventing intraoperative hypotension. Given its simplicity and broad availability, a mean arterial pressure alarm of 72 mmHg represents a pragmatic and cost-effective alternative for proactive blood pressure management.

title: Antibiotic prophylaxis with vancomycin and gentamicin and the occurrence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass
authors: Stefan Andrei; Sophie Provenchère; Anne Boutten; Kevin Boussion et al.
abstract: BACKGROUND Vancomycin combined with gentamicin (VGA) is used as an alternative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery when cephalosporins are contraindicated. However, the nephrotoxic potential of this combination raises concerns regarding postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI). OBJECTIVE This study aimed to evaluate the association between VGA prophylaxis and AKI occurrence in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), while accounting for preoperative risk factors. DESIGN Retrospective single-centre study. AKI was defined according to KDIGO criteria within 7 postoperative days. PATIENTS Of the 8895 eligible patients between April 2013 and December 2021, 8198 were included. Subgroup analyses were performed according to preoperative AKI risk status (high-risk: insulin-dependent diabetes, cirrhosis, acute endocarditis, preoperative critical state, emergency surgery, or cardiac transplantation). RESULTS In our cohort, 7469 (91%) received cephalosporins and 729 (9%) received VGA. The overall AKI incidence was 16%. AKI occurred more frequently in the VGA group (29% vs. 15%, P < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, VGA remained independently associated with AKI [odds ratio (OR) 1.29, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03 to 1.62, P = 0.024], confirmed by propensity score analysis (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.60, P = 0.005). In subgroup analyses, VGA was significantly associated with AKI in high-risk patients (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.04, P = 0.004), but not in low-risk patients (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.64, P = 0.285). CONCLUSION In this large retrospective cohort, VGA antibiotic prophylaxis was independently associated with increased AKI risk following cardiac surgery with CPB. This association was driven primarily by patients with preoperative risk factors for AKI. Alternative prophylactic regimens should be considered in high-risk patients when possible.

title: Effects of Ketamine and Esketamine on Postoperative Delirium After General Anesthesia: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression Analysis
authors: Shuying Li; Wenqin Zhou; Ping Li; Yajiao Hu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious complication, particularly in older adults undergoing major surgery. Pharmacologic prevention remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether perioperative ketamine or esketamine reduces POD incidence and to explore optimal administration strategies. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from inception to January 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing perioperative ketamine or esketamine with placebo or standard care. The primary outcome was POD incidence (risk ratio [RR]). Subgroup, meta‑regression, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) were performed. Sensitivity analyses addressed active comparators and unit‑of‑analysis issues. RESULTS: Twenty-five RCTs (3344 patients) were included (ketamine: 9; esketamine: 16). Both agents reduced POD risk versus control (ketamine: RR 0.69, 95% CI, 0.49–0.98, P = .04; esketamine: RR 0.58, 95% CI, 0.36–0.95, P = .03). Benefit was more evident with high-dose regimens (single bolus: ketamine >0.5 mg/kg or esketamine >0.25 mg/kg; cumulative dose: ketamine >1.0 mg/kg or esketamine >0.5 mg/kg), bolus-plus-infusion, and in major surgery. The effect was observed when POD was assessed 2 to 7 days postoperatively, but not within 24 hours. TSA indicated that current evidence remains inconclusive due to insufficient information size. Dizziness risk increased (RR 1.45, 95% CI, 1.14–1.84, P = .002), while postoperative depressive symptoms decreased (RR 0.78, 95% CI, 0.63–0.96, P = .02; based on 2 studies, 493 patients). CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative ketamine and esketamine show a potential signal for POD reduction, particularly with optimized dosing in high‑risk patients. However, the evidence is currently inconclusive, and increased dizziness risk precludes routine recommendation. Large, multicenter RCTs are urgently needed.

title: Impact of opioid-free general anesthesia with locoregional blocks during breast cancer surgery on systemic inflammatory response: results from a randomized controlled trial
authors: Brescia, F., Favero, A., Segatto, I., Massarut, S., Zanier, C., Fabiani, F., Nadalini, E., Morabito, A., Montico, M., Zucchetto, A., Zanussi, S., Baldassarre, G., Belletti, B.
abstract: Background For breast cancer patients with localized disease, surgery remains a cornerstone of treatment. Anesthesia during surgery is essential for pain management and influences patient recovery. Opioid-free general anesthesia with locoregional blocks (OfGA), as an alternative to traditional opioid-based general anesthesia (GA), may improve patient outcomes. Methods We set up a randomized trial to compare the impact of different anesthetic approaches on post surgical inflammation in breast cancer patients undergoing quadrantectomy. Patients were randomized to receive GA (n=34) or OfGA (n=34). Blood samples were collected pre-surgery and 1 hour and 24 hours post-surgery. As primary endpoint, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) was calculated. As secondary endpoints we collected data on side effects, pain management, and circulating inflammatory cytokines. Results Patients of the GA arm displayed significantly increased NLR, both at 1 (median change +0.13, IQR 0.01 to 0.62, p<0.0001) and 24 (median change +0.64, IQR 0.28 to 1.03, p<0.0001) hours post-surgery, compared with baseline. On the contrary, the OfGA arm displayed stable or minimally increased NLR (median change -0.08, IQR -0.21 to 0.17, p=ns, at 1 hour; +0.11, IQR -0.11 to 0.36, p=ns, at 24 hours post-surgery). Circulating inflammatory cytokines aligned with NLR data, showing significant increases in key inflammatory factors in samples from the GA arm compared with the OfGA arm. Pain management was similar in both arms, but OfGA was better tolerated and elicited fewer side effects. Conclusions In breast cancer surgery, opioid-free general anesthesia combined with locoregional blocks was associated with a reduced postoperative inflammatory response compared with conventional opioid-based general anesthesia, without compromising pain control. Further research is needed to determine whether these biological effects translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. Trial registration number NCT04172220.
